title: It’s time the BBC slapped a tobacco-style warning on Chris Packham
snippet: As the vegan dictator continues to terrorise innocent sausage-munchers, his programmes should come with a 'viewer discretion advised' label.

See more Published 08 March 2026 4:00pm GMT Environmentalist Chris Packham has been busy again this week, doing his best to destroy UK livestock farming.This feels like the latest in a series of attempts to wreck Britain’s rural traditions. Indeed, so vociferous and regular are his bombastic and inflammatory outpourings on everything from trail hunting to pig farming that the Government must be eyeing him for a peerage. He provides that colourful, on-the-ground messaging that tallies well with Labour’s own official policies on non-urbanites.While the Government is busy targeting farmers with extermination by tax and bureaucracy – labyrinthine schemes and paperwork that can send even the jolliest fat-fingered agriculturalist to jump in front of their combine – Packham never fails to paint farmers and country-dwellers as welly-wearing Satans. Farmers protest in Westminster, central London, on Tuesday – ahead of Chancellor Rachel Reeves’s Spring Statement – against the Government’s plans to levy inheritance tax on farms Credit: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty This week’s targets were meat producers. Fresh from a rather unsuccessful YouTube documentary that he starred in, Greenwashed, which claims to confront “the existential ecological crises threatening our planet”, the 64-year-old summoned a pliant young hack, one Steph Spyro, known for trying to free penguins from aquariums.During her audience with Packham – who revels in an aura of saintliness, even posing last year beside a painting of himself depicted as St Francis of Assisi – he cast his thoughts on meat production.He talked of his vision “to have a whole series of stickers printed of animals kept in appalling conditions”, and how he would “stick them on the meat packets of supermarkets and see how people react”.One can indeed picture him doing this. As vegans go into supermarkets to open milk cartoons and pour the contents across the floor, so Packham – protected by an entourage of dreadlocked, white trustafarians – can shove his stickers on packs of meat.Packham went on to explain to the nodding Ms Spyro: “If [customers] pick it up and see a pig in a farrowing crate covered in its own excrement, blood and rolling on its own piglets, then are they going to buy and eat that? A percentage of people would be sufficiently empathetic that they would change their habit.” He compares the supposed impact to when customers are “buying cigarettes and looking at diseased lungs”.Packham, who converted from long-term vegetarianism to veganism in 2019, wishes to terrorise the innocent sausage-muncher and bacon-sarnie-consumer, rubbing their noses in the foul filth of cruel and immoral meat production.And, like the best vegans out there, he joyfully fetishises the farming of animals, frothing at the mouth as he describes what happens behind the closed doors and gates of British agriculture – a hellish story of relentless cruelty.
